text: Given an integer array nums, find the subarray with the largest sum, and return its sum.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a subarray is a contiguous run of elements, and it can't be empty. So I must pick at least one number. And I only return the sum, not the start and end index. Is that right?
Yes. Non-empty, contiguous, and just the sum.

Okay. That non-empty part matters a lot. If every number is negative, the answer is still one of those numbers — it is not zero. For example, negative three, negative one, negative two should give negative one. I'll keep that in mind. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The array has up to ten to the fifth numbers, and each value is between negative ten thousand and ten thousand.

Got it. Up to a hundred thousand numbers, so I want one pass. And the biggest possible sum is a hundred thousand times ten thousand, which is one billion. The int limit is about two point one billion, so a plain int is enough — no need for a sixty-four bit integer. Let me run through the example: negative two, one, negative three, four, negative one, two, one, negative five, four. The best part is four, negative one, two, one — index three through six. Its sum is four, minus one, plus two, plus one, which is six. Notice it keeps the negative one inside, because the numbers around it make up for it. So the expected answer is six. The other two examples: a single one gives one, and five, four, negative one, seven, eight gives twenty-three — the whole array.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to try every start index, then grow the end one step at a time and keep a running sum. That's quadratic time. It's correct, but at a hundred thousand elements it took about three point seven seconds when I timed it. Too slow. This problem reminds me of a one-pass dynamic program, which is Kadane's algorithm. The idea: look at the best subarray that ends right here, at the current index. It has only two choices. Either it extends the best subarray that ended one step before, or it restarts with just the current number. Nothing else can be better. The real answer is just the best of these ends-here values over all indexes.

Here's the plan. I keep two variables. Cur-L is the best sum of a subarray that ends at the current number, and max-L is the best sum I've seen anywhere so far. Max-L starts at the smallest possible int, cur-L starts at zero. For each number, cur-L becomes the larger of extend — the old cur-L plus the number — and restart, the number by itself. Then max-L takes the larger of itself and cur-L. At the end I return max-L. One thing worth flagging — when do I restart? Restarting beats extending exactly when cur-L is negative. So I drop the past only when the past sum is negative. It does not depend on whether the current number is negative. A common wrong idea is to reset whenever I see a negative number. Take two, negative one, two. That rule gives two, but the right answer is three — the negative one is worth keeping, because two minus one is still positive. One more thing worth flagging — max-L starts at the smallest int, not at zero. This is a correctness rule, not style. If I start it at zero, then an array holding just negative four returns zero, but the answer is negative four. Zero means pick nothing, and that's not allowed. The scary part is that starting at zero still passes all three official examples. In my brute-force check, it failed on every all-negative array, and only those. And the smallest int is safe here because I only compare with max-L — I never add to it, so it can't overflow. There's a trade-off here. The follow-up hints at divide and conquer. That's a nice idea, but it's n log n and more code. Kadane is linear time and constant space, so I'll go with Kadane first. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up — and I'll talk through it rather than read it line by line. Inside the function I declare two ints: max-L, set to the smallest possible int, and cur-L, set to zero. Then one loop over the numbers. First line: cur-L becomes the max of cur-L plus the number, or the number alone — extend or restart. Second line: max-L becomes the max of max-L and cur-L. After the loop I return max-L. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the order of the two lines in the loop. I update cur-L first, then max-L. So max-L always sees a subarray that includes the current number — that's what keeps the empty subarray out. If I swapped the two lines, the very first compare would use cur-L at zero, which is the empty subarray, and the single negative four would return zero again. Also, starting cur-L at zero is fine: on the first number, extend and restart are both just the first element.

Let's dry-run the code with example one: negative two, one, negative three, four, negative one, two, one, negative five, four. Expected output is six. The first number sets cur-L and max-L to negative two. At index one, extending gives negative one but restarting gives one, so I restart — cur-L and max-L are both one. At index two I extend into negative two, and max-L stays at one. Now the key row, index three. Coming in, cur-L is negative two — the past is negative, so it can only hurt. Extend gives two, restart gives four, so I restart at index three. That's exactly where the best subarray begins. After that cur-L never goes negative again, so I keep extending: three, five, six — and max-L peaks at six at index six, the window from three to six, which is four, negative one, two, one. At index seven the negative five drops cur-L to one. That's still positive, so I don't restart, but max-L stays at six. The last four brings cur-L back to five, still below six. So I return six. That matches. Let's also test with corner cases. All negative — negative three, negative one, negative two — gives negative one: every step restarts, and max-L keeps the biggest negative. That's the case the smallest-int start is for. A single one gives one, and a single zero gives zero — one element comes back as-is. Five, four, negative one, seven, eight gives twenty-three: cur-L goes five, nine, eight, fifteen, twenty-three, never restarting, so the whole array is the answer. Ten thousand first, then all negative ten thousands, gives ten thousand — the best is just the first number. And a hundred thousand copies of ten thousand gives one billion, which fits in an int; a hundred thousand copies of negative ten thousand gives negative ten thousand.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear — one pass, two max calls per number. The space complexity is constant — just two integers. In the worst case it's still exactly n steps: there's no early exit, but there's no extra work either. At a hundred thousand elements it ran in about a quarter of a millisecond, versus nearly four seconds for the quadratic brute force. Oh, one more thing — I'd test this against the brute force on lots of small arrays. That's how the max-L-starts-at-zero bug shows up. It hides from the official examples, but fails on every all-negative array.
Good. The follow-up asks for divide and conquer. How would that go?

I split the array in the middle. The best subarray is in one of three places: all in the left half, all in the right half, or crossing the middle. The left and right cases are recursive calls. For the crossing case, I take the best sum that ends at the middle going left, plus the best sum that starts right after the middle going right. That's one linear scan. So the cost is two subproblems of half the size plus linear work, which is n log n time, plus a logarithmic stack for the recursion. It's correct, but slower than Kadane. When I timed it at a hundred thousand elements, it took about one point six milliseconds, versus about a quarter of a millisecond for Kadane. So in practice I'd ship Kadane, and keep divide and conquer as the follow-up answer.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed it as the best subarray that ends here — extend or restart — and showed the restart depends on the sign of the past sum, not the current number, with two, negative one, two. You explained why max-L must start at the smallest int — a single negative four would give zero — even though zero passes all the official examples. And you checked that an int is enough at one billion, then compared Kadane with divide and conquer on real numbers. Good work.
